abstract: Many areas around the globe are experiencing warmer temperatures, more extreme drought, and wildfires because of climate change. Therefore, plant populations may experience strong natural selection on traits associated with adaptation to rapid change. One trait likely under selection is stomatal conductance, which determines the rate at which water vapor and carbon dioxide diffuse through the stomata and is sensitive to environmental factors such as drought, CO2, and vapor pressure deficit. The purpose of this study is to understand how plants respond both ecologically and evolutionarily to an extreme multiyear drought. Using six populations of a perennial herb (Mimulus cardinalis), we measured the evolution of operational stomatal conductance in pre-drought ancestral and post-drought descendant cohorts planted in three common gardens across the species' range. This design allowed us to test (1) whether stomatal conductance evolved in response to drought and (2) whether populations with greater genetic variance evolved more. Patterns consistent with drought escape were more common than patterns consistent with avoidance (6 versus 4 of 18 population-by-garden combinations), but evidence for evolutionary change in stomatal conductance was limited overall, and the extent of change was not correlated with genetic variance. These findings offer a framework for future research on stomatal traits and insight into the rate at which plants respond to environmental change.
